```{r}
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 12))

# later task reads its choices from your preregistration and fits against this.
euframes <- read_csv("data/EUframes_cy.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

# The preregister -> build -> run -> report helpers. Each fit they make is a

source("R/spec_tools.R")
```

## The claim, and what we are doing to it

The original author (OA) studied how citizens frame the European Union. One claim from their paper is our target:

> "… poor economic performances … decrease positive dimensions of EU framing" (Teney 2016: 619)

Operationalised the way the Multi100 project constrained it for its five analysts: does a country's **unemployment rate** (poor economic performance) lower the **cosmopolitan** dimension of EU framing (peace, democracy, free movement, cultural diversity, a stronger say in the world)? The published anchor result was a coefficient of −0.0034, t = −4.03.

You hold the data, the tools, and the workflow the project used – and the code you work through is the coordinator's own submitted analysis. You are analyst no. 6, and the question is: how robust is that number to *justifiable* alternative choices? Work through the seven tasks below in order, from vocabulary to a dot on the live class chart.

::: callout-tip
## How the tasks work

Every task is a callout box with instructions, a **TODO** you complete, and code chunks that **already run** – so the report renders from the first preview. You edit the prose blanks and, in Tasks 5 and 6, the code. The browser version of this same exercise is on the workshop site if you would rather not install anything; this workspace is the full IDE pipeline.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Task 1 – Concepts"}
**Before touching data, fix the vocabulary.** In the four scenarios below, three are doing one of our three R's, while one is doing something else entirely.

**TODO: read the four scenarios and fill in the gaps.**

***Scenario 1:*** A reviewer reruns the authors' Stata `.do` file on the authors' data and gets a *different* coefficient from the one printed in the paper. This is an example of \_\_\_\_\_\_, even though what they *tried* to do failed.
***Scenario 2:*** The analyst uses the authors' submitted replication dataset, but they re-implement the model in R instead of Stata and centre the predictor. Is this a case of \_\_\_\_\_\_ or \_\_\_\_\_\_?
***Scenario 3:*** A preregistered team tests the identical hypothesis on a *separate, much larger* dataset chosen to be theoretically equivalent, and gets results that contradict the original. Their conclusion is that the original analysis has failed to \_\_\_\_\_\_.
***Scenario 4:*** Instead of the survey data used by the original authors, another researcher tests the same underlying idea on social-media texts using a machine-learning classifier method that the original never used. To their surprise, the authors' original findings prove \_\_\_\_\_\_ and the researcher concludes that they provide a reliable middle-range theory of the phenomenon they investigate.

*(Answers: 1 reproducibility – the activity is reproducibility even though it failed to match, so the verdict is 'not reproduced'; 2 arguably still reproducibility, a grey area – re-implementing on the same data in different software is a re-computation, though centring the predictor and differing estimator implementations nudge toward robustness; 3 replicability – same question, independent new data; 4 generalisability – the impostor, new data and a new method at once.)*
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Task 2 – Get the data and look at it"}
The **EU-frames dataset** (`EUframes_cy.csv`) is the corrected country-year panel behind the whole exercise. It is already loaded as `euframes` in the setup chunk, and the copy in `data/` is byte-identical to the one published in the analyst's fork on OSF (osf.io/6zqct – "Multi100 \| Teney_EurSocioRev_2016 \| Analyst_C6HJR", main folder); the official Multi100 archival record is at osf.io/8rtwe.

**TODO:** run the chunks, then read the small-multiples figure. Which countries trend down over 2004–2013? Note one in a comment.

```{r}
#| label: count-data
# How many countries, how many years, how big is the panel?
euframes |>
  summarise(
    countries = n_distinct(cntry),
    years     = n_distinct(year),
    rows      = n()
  )
```

You should see **27 countries**, **10 years** (2004–2013), and **270 rows**. The outcome we care about first is `mcosmo` – the mean cosmopolitan framing of the EU in each country-year (a 0–1 scale). The predictor is `unemp`, the annual unemployment rate; `growth` is annual GDP growth, and `n_cy` counts the survey respondents behind each row. Every column is described in `data/EUframes_cy_codebook.md`.

```{r}
#| label: fig-cosmo-trend
#| fig-cap: "Mean cosmopolitan EU framing over time, by country – an echo of OA's Figure 1."
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 6
ggplot(euframes, aes(x = year, y = mcosmo)) +
  geom_line(colour = "grey55") +
  geom_point(size = 0.7) +
  facet_wrap(~ cntry, ncol = 6) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(2004, 2008, 2013)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Mean cosmopolitan framing (0–1)")
```

Most countries drift gently; a few move sharply around the 2009 crisis. That variation – within a country, over time – is exactly what the fixed-effects model in Task 3 uses.

*Practising the OSF pull (optional).* `R/get_data.R` fetches this file from the analyst's OSF fork the way a researcher would, with a workshop-site mirror as a fallback. It is not needed – the file already ships in `data/` – but running it proves you can pull a real published artefact:

```{r}
#| label: get-data
#| eval: false
# Optional: confirm data/EUframes_cy.csv from OSF (uses the local copy offline).
source("R/get_data.R")
```
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

::: {.callout-note title="Task 3 – Reproduce the recorded result"}
This is the **reproducibility** check. Fit the two-way fixed-effects model the Multi100 Task-2 constraints point to: cosmopolitan framing on grand-mean-centred unemployment, with country and year fixed effects. The target is **t = −3.804** (df = 233, N = 270) – the value on record for analyst C6HJR in the Multi100 dataset.

```{r}
#| label: fit-corrected
# Grand-mean centre unemployment, exactly as the submitted analysis did. With
# two-way fixed effects this shifts the intercept, not the slope or the t – it
# is the transformation the constrained specification names, so do it explicitly.
euframes <- euframes |> mutate(unemp_c = unemp - mean(unemp, na.rm = TRUE))

# fixest::feols – the bar separates the regression from the fixed effects.
m1 <- feols(mcosmo ~ unemp_c | cntry + year, data = euframes)

tidy(m1)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-corrected
#| tbl-cap: "The constrained model on the corrected EUframes_cy.csv."
modelsummary(
  list("two-way FE (fixest)" = m1),
  estimate  = "{estimate}",
  statistic = "t = {statistic}",
  gof_map   = c("nobs", "r.squared"),
  coef_rename = c("unemp_c" = "Unemployment (centred)")
)
```

The coefficient is **−0.00347** with **t = −3.804** – exactly the value recorded for analyst C6HJR, reproduced from the published data and the published model. `feols` reports classical (IID) standard errors by default when two fixed-effect dimensions are present, which is why it matches the `plm` value the analyst used to three decimals.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="The other number in the record – a story worth opening"}
There is a second number in this analysis's public trail: **t = −3.853**. It is what the *first* submitted pipeline produced, and the gap to the −3.804 you just reproduced has a story.

The as-submitted data-preparation script stacked sixteen Eurobarometer waves and read the EB 70.1 file (`ZA4819`) twice by mistake: once for 2008 (correct) and again in place of EB 72.4 (`ZA4994`) for 2009. The panel's 2009 rows were therefore a copy of the 2008 respondents – the two builds diverge on 2009 and nowhere else, and 2009 carried about half the respondents it should have. The analyst caught the slip during the project and corrected it; the recorded −3.804 comes from the corrected build – the very `EUframes_cy.csv` you are using.

The whole trail is public in the analyst's fork (osf.io/6zqct): the `moreh_rep/` folder preserves the as-submitted pipeline; `moreh_rep_vAPR2025/` holds the corrected script – annotated "APRIL 2025 – Mistake in dataset here; the dataset associated with 'eb724' should be 'ZA4994_v3-0-0.dta'" – together with the exported corrected dataset; and the main folder now carries `EUframes_cy.csv` itself, the exact file this report loads. The official Multi100 component (osf.io/8rtwe) preserved only the earlier, uncorrected folder.

Want to see it for yourself? `forensics.R` puts the as-submitted `rep_data.csv` (which gives −3.853) beside the corrected panel and localises the disagreement to 2009 in two short diffs. It is an optional exhibit, not a task – open it if you are curious.

Coding can go wrong – even during a reanalysis. Keeping materials open and well documented is what lets a mistake be spotted and corrected. That is reproducibility working, not failing.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Task 4 – Estimand and DAG"}
Before estimating, say *precisely* what you are estimating. An estimand has two parts: a **unit-specific quantity** and a **target population** (Lundberg et al. 2021). State it outside any model.

**TODO – complete the estimand sentence:**

> Unit-specific quantity: the change in \[\_\_\_\_\] for a one-point difference in \[\_\_\_\_\]. Target population: \[\_\_\_\_\].

*(A defensible filling: the change in mean cosmopolitan framing within a country-year, for a one-percentage-point difference in that country's unemployment rate; across EU member states, 2004–2013.)*

Now the identification assumptions. `R/dag_starter.R` builds a half-drawn DAG: the causal path and two confounder pairs are in; the more arguable arrows are listed as ready-to-paste lines. Open the file, uncomment any edges you believe, re-source it, and re-run `adjustmentSets()`.

```{r}
#| label: dag
#| fig-cap: "The starter DAG: unemployment → framing, with country and year as confounders."
#| fig-height: 5
source("R/dag_starter.R")
plot_dag(dag)
```

```{r}
#| label: adjustment-set
# What must we adjust for to identify the unemployment -> framing effect?
dagitty::adjustmentSets(dag, exposure = "unemployment", outcome = "framing")
```

The starter graph returns `{ country, year }` – exactly what the two-way fixed effects you fitted in Task 3 absorb: country fixed effects adjust for `country`, year fixed effects adjust for `year`. The DAG and the model encode the same identification claim.

**TODO – answer two questions in a sentence each:**

1.  What do **country** and **year** fixed effects adjust for, in plain terms? *(country-constant traits, and shocks common to all countries in a year)*
2.  What can they **not** fix? *(a time-varying, country-level confounder – e.g. GDP growth moving both unemployment and framing within a country over time)*

Whatever set your DAG returns becomes field 4 of your preregistration, next.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Task 5 – My preregistration"}
The point of preregistration is that you commit to a choice **before** you see what it does. It stops you quietly picking the specification that happens to give the answer you wanted. Here the commitment is real in a mechanical sense too: the choices you declare in the cell below are remembered by the session, and every later cell reads them from here – the model builder refuses code that deviates from them.

Make one choice on each axis of the specification menu – every axis is live, including the outcome **family** and the **predictor** – then run the cell. `claim_align <- TRUE` is the day's convention, applied automatically: negative framings are reverse-coded (1 − y) and growth's claim-expected sign is flipped, so 'supports the claim' reads as a negative sign for everyone.

Multi100's Task 2 fixed unemployment as the measure on a gaussian scale; this menu opens both. That is not a stretch beyond the project – Task 1 of Multi100 already shows three of the five analysts reaching for GDP-growth measures when the choice was theirs.
:::

::: {.callout-important title="How this block maps to a real preregistration"}
*A real preregistration, shortened. Each numbered comment maps to a question in the OSF "Preregistration Template from AsPredicted.org" (the eight-question short form). Because you are reanalysing data that already exist, field 2 also stands in for the prior-knowledge section of the secondary-data template (van den Akker et al. 2021) – the part AsPredicted leaves out.*
:::

```{r}
#| label: prereg
# ============================================================================
# MY PREREGISTRATION – one specification, declared before seeing its result
# ============================================================================
# 1. The claim I am testing: .................................................
# 2. The data + what I already know: EUframes_cy.csv (270 country-years,
#    public); I know the constrained baseline gives t = -3.804.
# 3. My one specification – one choice on each axis:

my_outcome     <- "mcosmo"     # mcosmo | mutil | mpos    (positive framings)
                               # mcomm  | mlib  | mneg    (negative framings)
my_family      <- "gaussian"   # gaussian | beta   (logit-link on the cell
                               #                    means; beta reports z)
my_predictor   <- "unemp"      # unemp | growth    (the claim-carrying measure)
my_pred_form   <- "raw"        # raw | log   (growth: raw only; centring or
                               #              z-scaling would leave t, r and p
                               #              unchanged - not separate analyses)
my_copredictor <- "none"       # none | growth (beside unemp) | unemp (beside growth)
my_estimator   <- "fe_twoway"  # fe_twoway | fe_country | re | pooled_cl
my_sample      <- "all"        # all | y2004_2008 | y2009_2013 | no_bailout | no_GR_ES
my_weights     <- "none"       # none | n_cy   (re is never weighted)

claim_align    <- TRUE         # the day's convention, applied automatically

# 4. Why these controls, in one DAG-grounded sentence: .......................
# 5. Supported if the claim-aligned coefficient is negative and p < .05;
#    undermined if non-significant or positive. I will report what I get.

prereg()   # checks every choice against the menu and records the declaration
```

An optional mirror form may be used to log preregistrations for the room – the link is shared in the session. It is not required: the cell above, rendered into this report, is your official preregistration.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

::: {.callout-note title="Task 6 – Build and run your specification"}
This is the **robustness** check, and it is the part your classmates cannot copy from you: together the room samples the multiverse of defensible analyses. You have declared your specification; now translate it into model syntax yourself.

Fill the outcome, the right-hand side, and the estimator code exactly as you preregistered them. `build_model()` knows your declaration and will not accept anything else; its error messages tell you what is off. Write the log form as `log(unemp)`, and add any co-predictor with `+`. You do **not** write the fixed-effects, clustering, or family syntax here – the estimator and family codes stand for it, and `run_spec()` expands them into the real fit.
:::

```{r}
#| label: build-model
my_model <- build_model(mcosmo ~ unemp, estimator = "fe_twoway")
```

When the model is accepted, run it. `run_spec()` fits your preregistered specification for real – the estimator, family, sample and weights all expand into the matching `fixest`, `plm`, `betareg` or `glmmTMB` call – and prints its claim-aligned result:

```{r}
#| label: run-spec
run_spec(my_model)
```

Read the output like an analyst: the coefficient and its claim-aligned partial *r* (below zero supports the claim). The five Multi100 analysts run from about the 16th percentile of the specification curve (the most strongly claim-supporting) to about the 68th (near the null); your result is about to join theirs on the class chart.

**A second specification?** Edit the preregistration cell, rerun `prereg()`, rebuild, rerun. The mechanics allow it – but the label changes: your *first* declaration was a preregistration; everything after it is exploration. Saying which is which, out loud, is the entire discipline the day is about.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

::: {.callout-note title="Task 7 – Report to the class chart"}
Your result travels to the room from your preregistered choices – there is nothing to fill in and nothing to transcribe. `report_result()` refits your declared specification, builds the spec label, and always submits on the claim-aligned scale the chart is drawn on. It prints your submission line and a pre-filled form link; open it and press **Send**. Your result appears as an open circle on the live Multiverse chart within seconds.
:::

```{r}
#| label: report
report_result()
```

Run this, then open the submission link it prints – your result lands as a dot on the live [Multiverse](https://codemoreh.github.io/applied-replication/results.html) chart. If the form will not open on your machine, read the printed numbers to the facilitator and your dot still lands.

::: {.callout-note title="Going further (optional)"}
Time to spare? Each of these is a real fit you can run in this workspace.

- **A second, exploratory specification.** Change one axis in the preregistration cell, rerun `prereg()`, `build_model()` and `run_spec()`, then `report_result()` it. Two points on the class multiverse instead of one – the first preregistered, the second explicitly exploratory.

- **The mirror-image expectation.** The claim is about *positive* framing. Preregister a **negative** dimension instead (`mneg`, or communitarian `mcomm`): if poor economic performance lowers positive framing, does it *raise* negative framing? With `claim_align <- TRUE` the reverse-coding (1 − y) is applied for you, so the result restates itself on the same scale as the rest of the curve.

- **Beyond unemployment.** Preregister `my_predictor <- "growth"` (GDP growth, the claim carrier for three of the five original analysts): the claim now expects a *positive* growth coefficient on the positive framings, and the sign convention flips once more automatically. The growth mirror of the Task-3 anchor (`mpos ~ growth + unemp`, two-way FE) gives b = +0.00167, t = 1.59 – non-significant.

- **The full SCORE dossier.** OA's paper went through all three Rs in the SCORE programme and got three different verdicts: its push-button reproduction **failed** (the author-provided Stata code referenced file names that did not match what was available), and its preregistered secondary-data replication returned a **sign flip** (a positive coefficient, b = 0.002, p = .046, in the opposite direction to the original). Explore reproduction, robustness, and replication side by side at <https://osf.io/h7432/>.
:::
